# JAR Data — Analysis of Defects and Penalties

## Introduction

This analysis is designed for **JAR** (*Just About Right*) data, in which subjects assess a sensory attribute using a *too little / just about right / too much* type of scale. In this function, the analysis focuses on **defects**, that is, on all levels different from the reference JAR level, and on their link with the liking score. It makes it possible to describe the stimuli according to their defects, to represent the stimuli and the defects in the same space, and then to estimate **liking penalties** associated with these defects.

**Why not use a standard alternative?**

A mean liking score by stimulus does not tell you which defects explain a decrease in liking. Nor does a simple reading of the JAR responses clearly distinguish what reflects a lack from what reflects an excess relative to the ideal level. Here, the function recodes each attribute around the level defined in **Coding of the JAR level**, constructs a stimuli × defects contingency table, and then calculates liking penalties relative to the set of stimuli as a whole.

## Understanding what is happening “under the bonnet”

### Recoding the JAR level

The function begins by using the value entered in **Coding of the JAR level** to redefine, in each variable of **Sensory Attributes**, the reference level. The default value is `"jar"`. All the other levels are then treated as **defects**, that is, as deviations from the level judged to be “just about right”.

### Constructing the defect frequency table

After this recoding, the function removes the reference level (“just about right”) and counts, for each stimulus, how many times each defect was observed. The result is a **stimuli × defects** table, which forms the basis for the description of the stimuli and the factor representation.

### Describing stimuli through the defects

From this table, the function applies a frequency-description procedure. For each stimulus, it identifies the defects that are significantly more or less associated than in the table as a whole. The logic is similar to that used for CATA data: the frequency of a defect for a given stimulus is compared with its overall frequency, and significant associations are reported with their frequencies, p-values and V-tests.

### Representing products according to the defects

The function then performs a **correspondence analysis** on the defect table and produces the graph entitled **Representation of the Products According to Defects**. This map represents the stimuli and the defects simultaneously in the same factor space, in order to visualise the proximities between defect profiles.

### Calculating penalties

The function calculates penalties from **Stimulus Effect**, **Subject Effect**, **Liking Variable** and **Sensory Attributes**. The penalty measures the loss in liking associated with a defect: it is the difference between the mean liking score of the subjects who selected the JAR level and that of the subjects who selected the defect level. This difference is calculated across all stimuli simultaneously, giving it an overall rather than a stimulus-specific interpretation.

> The penalty is a negative value: it represents a loss in liking. The larger the absolute value, the more penalising the defect is.

### A penalty graph for each stimulus

The function produces a penalty graph for **each** stimulus. The display order depends on the order of the levels of **Stimulus Effect** in jamovi. It is therefore possible to show another stimulus first by modifying the order of the levels in the **Data** tab.

## Expected data structure

The data must contain:

-   a categorical column for **Stimulus Effect**;
-   a categorical column for **Subject Effect**;
-   a numeric column for **Liking Variable**;
-   one or more categorical columns for **Sensory Attributes**.

Each row corresponds to the evaluation of a stimulus by a subject. The variables in **Sensory Attributes** must be factors, because the function modifies their reference level using **Coding of the JAR level**.

Before running the analysis in jamovi, check in the **Data** tab that:

-   **Stimulus Effect** is categorical;
-   **Subject Effect** is categorical;
-   **Liking Variable** is numeric;
-   all the variables in **Sensory Attributes** are categorical;
-   the JAR level used in your data matches exactly the value entered in **Coding of the JAR level**.

## Guide to the interface

The analysis appears in **SEDA \> Fixed List of Attributes \> Analysis of JAR Data**. The interface includes four variable drop zones, the **Read me before running** box, and the **Coding of the JAR level** text field.

### Variables to enter

#### Stimulus Effect

**Role:** identifies the stimuli to be analysed. **Impact on the calculation:** this variable defines the groups for which defect frequencies are calculated and for which penalty graphs are generated. **Practical advice:** the order of the levels of this variable determines the display order of the penalty graphs. Modify this order in the **Data** tab if you want to see a particular stimulus first.

#### Subject Effect

**Role:** identifies the subjects. **Impact on the calculation:** this variable is passed to the penalty calculation and is used to structure the observations by subject. **Practical advice:** check that the same subject keeps exactly the same identifier throughout the file.

#### Liking Variable

**Role:** contains the overall liking score used to calculate the penalties. **Impact on the calculation:** this is the numeric variable on which the function estimates the effect of the defects. The penalty measures the loss on this score. **Practical advice:** make sure that the liking scale is consistent for all stimuli and all subjects.

#### Sensory Attributes

**Role:** groups together the JAR variables, one per sensory attribute. **Impact on the calculation:** each variable is recoded around the level defined in **Coding of the JAR level**; all the other levels become defects. **Practical advice:** check that each variable does contain the JAR level with the exact expected label.

### Read me before running

**Role:** displays built-in help in the results. **Impact on the calculation:** no statistical effect. **Practical advice:** leave this option ticked for the first few uses. It is **enabled by default**.

### JAR level coding: Coding of the JAR level

**Role:** indicates the exact label of the level considered to be the reference JAR level. **Impact on the calculation:** this parameter determines the level removed from the defect table and used as the reference in the recoding. If the value does not match the data, the analysis may fail or produce inconsistent results. **Practical advice:** the default value is `jar`. Adapt it exactly to the label used in your file, respecting case.

## Step-by-step procedure

1.  Open your dataset in jamovi.
2.  In the **Data** tab, check that the stimulus variable is categorical, the subject variable is categorical, the liking variable is numeric, and that all the JAR variables are categorical.
3.  Note the exact label of the “just about right” level used in your JAR variables.
4.  Open **SEDA \> Fixed List of Attributes \> Analysis of JAR Data**.
5.  Place the stimulus variable in **Stimulus Effect**.
6.  Place the subject variable in **Subject Effect**.
7.  Place the liking variable in **Liking Variable**.
8.  Place all the JAR variables in **Sensory Attributes**.
9.  In **Coding of the JAR level**, enter the exact label of the JAR level; leave `jar` if that is indeed the label used in your data.
10. First read the defect frequency table to check the structure of the data.
11. Then consult the description of the stimuli according to the defects.
12. Examine the **Representation of the Products According to Defects** map for an overall view.
13. Read the penalty table, then the **Penalties for Product ...** graphs to identify the priority defects.

## Interpreting the results

### Frequency Table — defect frequency table

This table cross-tabulates the stimuli in rows and the non-JAR levels in columns. Each cell indicates the number of times a defect was observed for a given stimulus. It is the basis for all the subsequent outputs.

| Element | Meaning |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| High value in a cell | The defect is frequent for this stimulus |
| Row with several high values | The stimulus accumulates several frequent defects |
| High column for several stimuli | Frequent defect, but not necessarily specific |

> **Point of attention:** a very rare defect will contribute little to the interpretation. A column with very low frequencies generally indicates a weakly discriminating defect.

### Description of the Stimuli According to Defects

This table describes, stimulus by stimulus, the significantly associated defects.

| Element              | Meaning                                            |
|--------------------|----------------------------------------------------|
| *(first column)*       | Stimulus concerned                                 |
| **Defect**           | Characteristic defect                              |
| **Intern %r**        | Percentage of the defect for this stimulus         |
| **Global %**         | Overall percentage of the defect                   |
| **Intern frequency** | Absolute frequency of the defect for this stimulus |
| **Global frequency** | Total absolute frequency of the defect             |
| **p**                | P-value of the test                                |
| **Vtest**            | Standardised intensity of the association          |

-   A positive **V-test** indicates that the defect is over-represented for this stimulus.
-   A negative **V-test** indicates that it is under-represented — which is also informative.
-   A low **p-value** indicates a clearer association.

> A stimulus absent from this table shows no defect significantly associated at the threshold used: its defect profile is close to the mean of all the stimuli.

### Representation of the Products According to Defects — graph

This graph is derived from the correspondence analysis of the defect table. It represents the stimuli and the defects simultaneously in the same factor space. Two nearby stimuli have similar defect profiles; a defect close to a stimulus is more strongly associated with it. The percentage displayed on each axis indicates the share of information captured by that dimension.

This map provides an overall view, to be complemented by the description table for the statistical detail.

### Penalty Table — Penalties Obtained from All Defects

This table presents, for each defect, the estimated effect on the liking score.

| Element        | Meaning                                              |
|----------------|------------------------------------------------------|
| **Defect** | Defect concerned                                     |
| **Penalty**    | Estimated loss in liking associated with this defect |
| **Std. Error** | Standard error of the estimate                       |
| **p**          | P-value of the test                                  |

-   The larger the absolute value of **Penalty**, the stronger the estimated effect.
-   A low **p-value** suggests an effect more clearly highlighted by the data.
-   A weakly significant penalty does not necessarily imply the absence of an effect: the defect may simply be too rare to be estimated precisely.

### Penalties for Product ... — graphs by stimulus

The function generates a penalty graph for each stimulus. The x-axis corresponds to the frequency of the defect for that stimulus; the y-axis to the penalty calculated across all stimuli. Error bars are drawn around the points, defects with p \< 0.05 are highlighted visually, and labels appear for defects with p \< 0.20.

| Element | Meaning |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| High frequency + marked penalty | Priority defect: frequent and strongly penalising |
| High frequency + weak penalty | Frequent but less penalising defect |
| Low frequency + marked penalty | Rare but potentially problematic defect |
| Low frequency + weak penalty | Secondary defect |

> **Point of attention:** the graph combines **local** information (the frequency of the defect for the displayed stimulus) with **overall** information (the penalty calculated across all stimuli). This point is essential in order not to over-interpret an isolated point on the graph.

## Worked example

The **milkshake** dataset concerns three products (`284`, `859`, `972`) evaluated using several JAR attributes related in particular to odour, texture, fluidity, sweetness, and acidity. It is used here as an illustration to help read the outputs of the function. The frequencies, V-tests, and penalties reported below come directly from the results provided.

### Recommended settings

| Option                      | Value                                  |
|-----------------------------|-----------------------------------------|
| **Stimulus Effect**         | Product |
| **Subject Effect**          | Panelist |
| **Liking Variable**         | Liking |
| **Sensory Attributes**      | all JAR variables from Color to Taste_Van |
| **Coding of the JAR level** | `jar` |

### Reading the Frequency Table (Stimuli × Defects)

The frequency table shows that the three products have very different defect profiles.

**Product 859** is strongly marked by *Not_enough_texture* (**38 subjects out of 47**, i.e. **80.85%**) and *Too_fluid* (**70.21%**); these are the two most frequent defects in the whole dataset.

**Product 972** stands out mainly through *Not_enough_odor_int* (**53.19%**), *Not_enough_odor_fruit* (**46.81%**), *Not_enough_odor_van* (**44.68%**), and *Too_much_sweetness* (**42.55%**).

**Product 284** shows several frequent but less extreme defects: *Not_enough_texture* (**57.45%**), *Not_enough_odor_int* (**48.94%**), *Too_fluid* (**46.81%**), and *Not_enough_odor_van* (**44.68%**).

This first reading is important: it helps identify which defects dominate sensorially for each product, even before knowing whether they are actually associated with a drop in liking.

### Reading the Description of the Products According to Defects

The table identifies the defects that are significantly over- or under-represented for each product relative to the overall mean.

**Product 859** is the one whose profile stands out most clearly. It is more strongly associated with *Not_enough_texture* (**p = 0.055, V-test = 1.92**) and *Too_fluid* (**p = 0.080, V-test = 1.75**). Conversely, it is significantly less associated with *A_little_plain* (**p = 0.040, V-test = -2.05**) and *Not_enough_odor_van* (**p = 0.049, V-test = -1.97**). Its sensory identity is therefore mainly driven by texture and fluidity defects rather than by a lack of vanilla odour.

**Product 972** is more strongly associated with *Too_much_sweetness* (**p = 0.087, V-test = 1.71**), but the positive associations remain modest at the 5% threshold. It is, however, under-represented for *Not_enough_texture* (**p = 0.072, V-test = -1.80**) and *Not_enough_sweetness* (**p = 0.099, V-test = -1.65**), which places it in partial opposition to 859 on these dimensions.

**Product 284** appears much closer to the overall mean profile. In the displayed results, no defect stands out clearly at the 5% threshold, suggesting a less specific product than the other two from the point of view of its dominant defects.

### Reading the Representation of the Products According to Defects graph

The first dimension explains **74.78%** of the inertia and clearly opposes **859** to **972**. On the **859** side, the main defects are *Too_fluid*, *Not_enough_texture*, and *Not_enough_sweetness*. On the **972** side, the main defects are *Too_much_sweetness*, *Too_much_odor_van*, and *Not_enough_odor_fruit*. **284** occupies an intermediate position, slightly on the side of *A_little_plain* and some defects related to fruity or vanilla odours. The second dimension (**25.22%**) refines these oppositions, especially around *Too_much_texture* and *Too_much_acidity*.

This map does not replace the tables, but it makes it possible to visualise in a single figure the overall opposition between the defect profiles of the three products.

### Reading the Penalties Obtained from All Defects table

The penalty table provides a **global** reading of the effect of defects on liking, across all products taken together. It does not say how often a defect appears for a given product; it indicates how strongly that defect is associated with an average loss in liking when it is observed.

In this example, only one defect is significant at the 5% threshold: **Too_much_odor_fruit**, with a penalty of **-2.67** and a **p-value of 0.018**. It is therefore the only defect whose negative effect on liking is clearly supported by the data. Several other defects show notable penalties without reaching this threshold, for example **Too_much_acidity** (**-4.03**, p = **0.082**), **Too_much_texture** (**-1.78**, p = **0.089**), and **Not_enough_acidity** (**-1.03**, p = **0.087**). They cannot be regarded as statistically significant here, but they remain weak signals worth monitoring.

> **Point of attention:** penalties are calculated across all three products simultaneously. They measure **global** information — which defect costs the most in liking, across all products combined — rather than **local** information — how often that defect appears for a given product. It is precisely the combination of these two readings that is useful.

### Reading the Penalties for Product 284, 859 and 972 graphs

These three graphs combine two complementary pieces of information:

-   on the **x-axis**, the frequency of the defect for the product considered;
-   on the **y-axis**, the global penalty associated with that defect.

In other words, a given defect keeps the **same y-coordinate** from one graph to another because its penalty is global, but it changes its x-coordinate depending on how frequent it is for the product displayed. The red points correspond to defects whose penalty is significant; here, this is essentially **Too_much_odor_fruit**.

For **product 284**, *Too_much_odor_fruit* appears as a penalising defect, but it remains **rare** (**6.38%**). By contrast, *Not_enough_odor_int* (**48.94%**), *Too_fluid* (**46.81%**), *Not_enough_odor_van* (**44.68%**), and *Not_enough_texture* (**57.45%**) are much more frequent, without being associated with a significant penalty. The graph therefore suggests a product that accumulates several perceived defects, but without a strong hedonic cost being clearly demonstrated for the most frequent ones.

For **product 859**, the reading is particularly striking: *Not_enough_texture* (**80.85%**) and *Too_fluid* (**70.21%**) are by far the most frequent defects. Yet their global penalties remain modest and non-significant, at **-0.43** and **-0.46** respectively. This makes them defects that are **highly visible sensorially**, but **not strongly penalising** in the liking data. By contrast, *Too_much_odor_fruit* remains the most penalising defect at the global level, while being very infrequent here (**4.26%**). The graph therefore clearly shows that a very frequent defect is not necessarily the one that should be corrected first if the main aim is to improve liking.

For **product 972**, the profile is different. The most frequent defects are *Not_enough_odor_int* (**53.19%**), *Not_enough_odor_fruit* (**46.81%**), *Not_enough_odor_van* (**44.68%**), and *Too_much_sweetness* (**42.55%**). However, *Too_much_sweetness* has a **positive** penalty (**0.43**), which indicates that it is not associated here with a drop in liking. *Too_much_odor_fruit*, the only globally significant penalising defect, is again very rare for this product (**4.26%**). The graph therefore suggests that 972 shows several deviations from the JAR level, but without any defect that is both very frequent and clearly penalising.

### Synthetic interpretation

This example clearly illustrates the value of the function and the logic of reading it in two stages. The frequency table and the product descriptions make it possible to identify the most present and most structuring defects for each product. The product × defects map provides an overall view of the oppositions, while the penalty table identifies the defects whose impact on liking is strongest, regardless of their frequency. The product-specific graphs are where these two readings truly come together: a defect that is both frequent and penalising is a priority, a penalising but rare defect should be monitored, and a frequent but only weakly penalising defect may be less urgent.

> **What this example shows:** JAR analysis is not only used to identify the most frequent defects, but also to distinguish those that are **frequent**, those that are **penalising**, and above all those that are **both**. It is this combination that makes it possible to prioritise product optimisation actions.

## Practical advice

-   Always check that **Coding of the JAR level** exactly matches the label used in your data, including case.
-   Make sure that all JAR variables are indeed categorical in jamovi before running the analysis.
-   Always read the frequency table before interpreting the penalties: a high penalty on a very rare defect is difficult to use in product optimisation.
-   Focus first on defects that are both frequent and associated with a marked and significant penalty.
-   Do not over-interpret a weakly significant penalty as a total absence of effect.
-   Bear in mind that the penalty is calculated overall across all the stimuli, whereas the frequency shown in the graph is local to the displayed stimulus.
-   Use the **Representation of the Products According to Defects** map for the overall view, and the tables for the detail.
-   If you want another stimulus to be displayed first in the penalty graphs, modify the order of the levels of **Stimulus Effect** in the **Data** tab.

## In summary

This analysis turns JAR responses into a structured reading of perceived defects and their link with liking. It combines a **defect frequency table**, a **description of the stimuli according to the defects**, a **factor representation of the products and defects**, and then an **estimation of the penalties** associated with each defect. Its main interest lies in relating, within the same framework, the frequency of deviations from the ideal level and their potential cost in terms of liking, in order to guide product optimisation in a way that is both descriptive and quantitative.
